questions.Source/Guideline: Early Detection of Prostate Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A 76-year-old man in excellent health has PSA 0.8 ng/mL and asks whether to continue screening. What is the most guideline-concordant counseling?
questions.Option A: Stop screening solely because he turned 75
questions.Option B: Personalize continued screening based on health, PSA, risk, life expectancy, and preferences
questions.Option C: Switch from PSA to urine cytology
questions.Option D: Proceed to biopsy because screening age is advanced
questions.Option E: Use PSA velocity alone to decide
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. Screening decisions in older patients should be individualized using shared decision-making, PSA level, overall risk, life expectancy, general health, and patient preference. Option A is incorrect because age alone is not the entire decision framework. Option C is incorrect because urine cytology is not a prostate cancer screening test. Option D is incorrect because age does not itself mandate biopsy, especially with a low PSA. Option E is incorrect because PSA velocity should not be the sole trigger for further testing. Teaching point: In older screening candidates, the senior-level decision is whether continued detection would plausibly improve outcomes, not whether an age cutoff automatically controls care. Source: American Urological Association. Early Detection of Prostate Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A man previously treated with definitive radiation has rising PSA and a focal PET-avid prostate lesion. He wants local salvage ablation. What is required before local salvage therapy?
questions.Option A: Treat based on PET positivity alone
questions.Option C: Start prostate bed radiation as after prostatectomy
questions.Option D: Use PSA velocity as tissue confirmation
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. Local salvage therapy after primary radiation should be performed only after pathologic confirmation of recurrent prostate cancer, because imaging can be false positive and the extent of recurrence affects treatment choice. Option A is incorrect because PET positivity alone is insufficient. Option C is incorrect because prostate bed radiation logic applies after prostatectomy, not after prior definitive radiation. Option D is incorrect because PSA kinetics cannot prove local histology. Option E is incorrect because chemotherapy is not the diagnostic prerequisite for local salvage selection. Teaching point: After radiation failure, local salvage is a tissue-confirmed recurrence pathway, not an imaging-only reflex. Source: American Urological Association. Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A patient with intermediate-risk NMIBC has a complete response to induction BCG, and BCG supply is adequate. Which maintenance plan is appropriate?
questions.Option A: Maintenance BCG for one year as tolerated
questions.Option B: Maintenance BCG for three years by default
questions.Option D: Single postoperative chemotherapy instead of maintenance
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. An intermediate-risk patient who completely responds to induction BCG may receive maintenance BCG for one year as tolerated when BCG is available. Option B is incorrect because three-year maintenance is the high-risk complete-response strategy. Option C is incorrect because complete response does not mandate cystectomy. Option D is incorrect because single postoperative chemotherapy is a perioperative recurrence-reduction maneuver, not the maintenance plan after induction BCG response. Option E is incorrect because surveillance remains necessary. Teaching point: BCG maintenance duration is risk-stratified; intermediate-risk complete responders are not managed with the same duration as high-risk complete responders. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A recurrent uric acid stone former has persistently acidic urine and no calcium stone risk factors requiring thiazide. Which prevention strategy is first-line?
questions.Explanation: Option C is correct. Uric acid stone prevention centers on urinary alkalinization, commonly with potassium citrate, because uric acid solubility is strongly pH dependent. Option A is incorrect because acetohydroxamic acid is an adjunct for selected struvite stones when surgical options are exhausted. Option B is incorrect because calcium elimination is not uric-acid directed and may increase calcium oxalate risk. Option D is incorrect because antibiotics do not correct uric acid supersaturation. Option E is incorrect because cystine-binding thiol drugs are used for cystinuria after appropriate non-thiol measures fail. Teaching point: Uric acid stones are primarily a urine-pH problem; alkalinization is more targeted than calcium or infection-stone therapies. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A recurrent stone former starts diet changes and medication based on metabolic testing. What follow-up best checks whether the prevention plan changed urinary risk?
questions.Option D: Repeat a 24-hour urine collection within six months
questions.Option E: Bone scan after each dose adjustment
questions.Explanation: Option D is correct. After initiating stone-prevention treatment, repeat 24-hour urine testing within about six months assesses response and guides further adjustment. Option A is incorrect because cytology evaluates urothelial malignancy risk, not metabolic stone risk. Option B is incorrect because symptom resolution does not prove metabolic risk correction. Option C is incorrect because cystoscopy does not measure urinary supersaturation or medication response. Option E is incorrect because bone scan is not used to titrate stone-prevention therapy. Teaching point: Metabolic stone prevention is measured, not assumed; repeat urine chemistry confirms whether the selected intervention changed the risk profile. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
questions.Question: A patient labeled as OAB records 4 L/day intake, high urine output, large voided volumes, and few urgency leaks. What is the best use of this diary?
questions.Option E: Address polyuria and fluid drivers before OAB escalation
questions.Explanation: Option E is correct. A diary showing high intake, high urine output, and large voided volumes should shift attention toward polyuria or fluid-behavior drivers before escalating idiopathic OAB therapy. Option A is incorrect because procedural escalation should not precede phenotype clarification when the diary suggests a non-OAB driver. Option B is incorrect because chronic catheter drainage is not treatment for intake-related frequency. Option C is incorrect because cytology does not grade urgency or quantify urine production. Option D is incorrect because cystectomy is not an appropriate response to a diary-driven polyuria pattern. Teaching point: The value of a bladder diary is not just counting voids; it can prevent misclassification of global polyuria as refractory OAB. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

questions.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
questions.Question: A severely impacted idiopathic OAB patient has failed behavioral, medication, and minimally invasive options or is not a candidate for them. Which high-morbidity option may be discussed?
questions.Option A: Augmentation cystoplasty or urinary diversion in selected cases
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. For rare, severely impacted patients who fail, cannot tolerate, or are not candidates for other OAB therapies, augmentation cystoplasty or urinary diversion may be discussed after careful counseling. Option B is incorrect because cytology does not treat storage symptoms. Option C is incorrect because antibiotics do not treat idiopathic urgency without infection. Option D is incorrect because bone scan does not manage refractory OAB. Option E is incorrect because ureteroscopy does not reduce detrusor overactivity. Teaching point: Major reconstructive options sit at the far end of the OAB algorithm and are reserved for exceptional refractory cases, not routine third-line escalation. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

questions.Question: A 72-year-old smoker on apixaban has confirmed microhematuria on microscopy. How should anticoagulation affect the hematuria evaluation?
questions.Option A: Evaluate using the same risk-based approach as patients not taking anticoagulants
questions.Option B: Attribute hematuria to apixaban and stop evaluation
questions.Option D: Treat empirically with antibiotics without culture
questions.Option E: Use urine cytology as the complete evaluation
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. Patients with microhematuria who take anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents should undergo the same risk-based evaluation as patients not taking those agents. Option B is incorrect because anticoagulation can reveal bleeding from underlying pathology and should not end the workup. Option C is incorrect because microhematuria requires microscopic evaluation, not dipstick alone. Option D is incorrect because antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection. Option E is incorrect because cytology alone is not a complete hematuria evaluation. Teaching point: Anticoagulant use is not an explanation that cancels hematuria risk stratification; it should not shortcut malignancy evaluation. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A man with CP/CPPS and bothersome LUTS asks about tadalafil. He has no nitrate use and understands the evidence is symptom-directed. What is reasonable?
questions.Option A: Tadalafil is reserved for culture-proven prostatitis
questions.Option D: Daily tadalafil may be prescribed for prostatitis symptoms
questions.Explanation: Option D is correct. Daily tadalafil may be prescribed for CP/CPPS prostatitis symptoms, with or without concomitant erectile dysfunction, after appropriate counseling and phenotype-directed selection. Option A is incorrect because the CP/CPPS tadalafil pathway does not require culture-proven infection. Option B is incorrect because repeated antibiotics after negative cultures add harm without treating demonstrated infection. Option C is incorrect because long-term systemic glucocorticoids should be avoided for male chronic pelvic pain syndromes. Option E is incorrect because cystectomy is not a treatment for CP/CPPS symptom control. Teaching point: CP/CPPS management is phenotype-directed; tadalafil is a reasonable selected option for prostatitis symptoms and LUTS rather than an antimicrobial substitute. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline
questions.Question: A woman with recurrent uncomplicated UTI wants D-mannose alone because she hopes to avoid antibiotics. What counseling best matches current guidance?
questions.Option D: D-mannose is preferred over vaginal estrogen in postmenopause
questions.Option E: D-mannose alone may not be effective for prevention
questions.Explanation: Option E is correct. Patients with recurrent UTI should be informed that D-mannose alone may not be effective for prophylaxis, based on contemporary evidence showing no clear recurrence benefit. Option A is incorrect because prevention supplements do not replace culture-guided treatment of symptomatic acute episodes. Option B is incorrect because D-mannose does not require fluoroquinolone exposure. Option C is incorrect because D-mannose use does not require surveillance cystoscopy. Option D is incorrect because vaginal estrogen remains a recommended prevention option for peri- and postmenopausal patients without contraindication. Teaching point: Nonantibiotic prevention counseling should distinguish low-harm interest from proven efficacy; D-mannose is not a high-confidence standalone prevention strategy. Source: American Urological Association. Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline.
